title: The sweeper is up and lethal is one Vampire away: fire now, or wait for the bigger count?

board.you: Turn 7, precombat main, 29 life, land drop already made. Battlefield: Corpse Knight, Mondrak, Glory Dominus, Blood Artist, Cruel Celebrant, Legion Lieutenant, and four 1/1 black Vampire tokens — 2/2s under Legion Lieutenant's anthem. Also Arcane Signet and six untapped lands: Command Tower, Godless Shrine, Blood Crypt, Sacred Foundry, Swamp, Plains. Seven mana available. Edgar Markov is in the command zone.
board.table: Player 2 (Azorius control) is at 33 with five untapped lands and nothing on the battlefield. Stated assumption: a control seat at this bracket sitting on five untapped lands after seven turns of doing nothing is holding a sweeper, and that sweeper is sorcery-speed. Player 3 (Rakdos midrange) is at 3, tapped out, with a lone 5/5 — your engine put them there. Player 4 (Simic ramp) is at 38 with two untapped lands and two ground blockers, a 4/4 and a 2/2.

scenario.extras: Corpse Knight converts and Mondrak doubles, so one Vampire spell cast is one eminence token doubled to two, then the creature itself — three separate creature entries, three Corpse Knight triggers, three life from every opponent. Verified stack 009 counted this entry shape; verified stack 002 is where the doubling math sits on the record. Corpse Knight causes life loss rather than damage, so nothing about it can be prevented or redirected. Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant are the mirror image: they pay nothing on the way in and everything on the way out — each of your creatures that dies is one life off the table per drain, and both drains keep firing even in the wipe that kills them. Last, know what your own Olivia's Wrath eats: five of the twenty-nine creatures in your 99 are not Vampires, and two of them — Corpse Knight and Mondrak — are standing on this battlefield right now.
scenario.question: Player 3 is at three and one Vampire spell kills them outright. Player 2 has held five lands for two turns. Do you cast the Knight now and take the kill on a three-trigger count, hold the card and go bigger next turn, or cast the Knight and clear the ground with your own Olivia's Wrath?

branches.choice: Cast Knight of the Ebon Legion, take the kill, and turn the tokens toward Player 2
branches.line:
One black mana. The eminence trigger makes a token, Mondrak makes it two, and those two plus the Knight are three creature entries. Corpse Knight fires three times: every opponent loses three, and Player 3 was at three. Gone before you touch combat.

Attack Player 2 with the four 2/2 tokens and Legion Lieutenant. They control no creatures, so that is ten unblocked damage and the seat holding the sweeper goes from thirty to twenty. Leave Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant home.

Spend two of the remaining six on Night's Whisper, then keep {2}{B} up so the Knight can become a 4/5 with deathtouch on somebody else's turn. Player 2 lost thirteen, so the Knight banks a counter at your end step too. You end with a card in hand, an engine intact, twelve creatures, and one fewer opponent.
branches.signals:
Killing a player who is at three is the least controversial kill in Commander. Nobody at the table thinks you were unfair; two of them are quietly relieved.

The tokens pointed at the control seat are the real statement. You are telling Player 2 that their sweeper is now a defensive card.

And the two drains standing untapped behind the attack say the rest. A control player who reads boards for a living will count your creatures, look at Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant, and realize the wipe has a price tag with their name on it.
branches.coalition_risk:
Moderate and shrinking. You remove a seat, and the two who remain have twenty and thirty-five life — neither of them feels like the game just ended.

The cost is that Player 2 now has a reason to wrath on their own turn rather than wait for a better one. Accept that — better, welcome it. On this board their sweeper is twelve deaths, and every one of those deaths pays you through both drains.

Player 4 stays comfortable and unbothered, which is exactly where you want the ramp deck while you are trading with the control deck.
branches.coaching:
Take the kill. Always, when it costs one mana.

Attack Player 2, not Player 4. Player 4 has thirty-eight life and two blockers; Player 2 has no creatures and the one card that unmakes your board. Ten across the red zone turns their sweeper from a tempo play into a panic button.

Now do their math. You end on twelve creatures, and Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant see every death including their own: death triggers look back at the board before the wipe. Twelve deaths is twelve off each opponent from Celebrant, twelve more from Blood Artist pointed anywhere you like, and twenty-four life to you. Aim them all at the caster and a resolved wrath takes Player 2 from twenty to negative four on their own card. Say none of this out loud. Let them count it.

Yes, you are feeding a board a sweeper is coming for: one mana of board, and it removes a player. If the wrath comes anyway, Edgar walks in next turn on six of your seven-plus mana, and every cheap Vampire after him is two bodies again.

Keep Olivia's Wrath in hand for whatever Player 2 rebuilds into — worth far more at their board.

Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities
buy resilience instead of restraint where you can

branches.choice: Hold the Knight and pass with seven mana up
branches.line:
Cast nothing. Keep Knight of the Ebon Legion in hand so a sweeper cannot two-for-one you, leave the board exactly as the table has already priced it, and plan to go next turn with eight mana — the Knight plus Olivia's Wrath in one turn, or whatever the draw step adds to the count.

Player 3 survives at three. Player 2 untaps with five lands and a board they have had a full rotation to plan against.
branches.signals:
Passing with seven untapped is meant to read as held interaction. Now look at your hand: a creature and two sorceries. There is not one instant in it.

A control player who has been counting your mana since turn three reads that bluff correctly, and the read they take away is that you flinched. That is the most expensive free information you can give a draw-go seat.
branches.coalition_risk:
Lowest this turn and highest across the next one. Player 3 lives at three, and a midrange deck with nothing left to lose spends its turn making somebody else's problem worse — usually yours, because your board is the one that killed them.

And you hand Player 2 the cleanest possible wrath window: your board at its current size, your payoff cards unspent, and a full turn to find a second answer for whatever you deploy after.
branches.coaching:
This is the branch that loses quietly. Exactly how:

Holding is meant to buy insurance against the wipe. It is already in play. Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant turn every death into drain, and they fire even as they die: death triggers look back at the board before the sweeper. Buy resilience instead of restraint — you already did. Now spend it.

The insurance you hope to draw is not coming: you hold protection by turn six in half your games, and this hand is the other half. Nothing here answers a wrath, so the extra turn buys a bigger board to lose, not a safer one.

Against control, holding back is the loss: buying time is their plan, and every turn you do not convert brings the card that blanks your board.

Hand discipline is real here: eminence pays you for emptying your hand, so overcommitting is the failure mode stitched in. But discipline means holding when committing buys nothing. Take this branch the day the extra turn buys a bigger count: a second converter in hand, or a doubler you have not deployed. You have neither. What you have is a one-mana spell that kills a player.

citations.quote: The artifact’s ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its owner’s graveyard at the same time as the creatures.
against a control deck, holding back often IS the loss, because buying time is exactly their plan

branches.choice: Cast the Knight, then clear the ground with your own Olivia's Wrath
branches.line:
Knight for one, Olivia's Wrath for five. Player 3 dies to the Corpse Knight triggers first, so their 5/5 leaves the game with them — leaves, not dies, so your drains see nothing.

The Wrath resolves with ten Vampires on your side — four old tokens, two new, the Knight, Legion Lieutenant, Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant — so every non-Vampire takes minus ten minus ten: Player 4's 4/4 and 2/2, and your own Corpse Knight and Mondrak. Four deaths. Cruel Celebrant sees your two and takes two off each opponent, Blood Artist sees all four and sends four more wherever you point; you gain six.

Swing the four tokens, Legion Lieutenant, Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant into an empty board for thirteen, putting Player 4 near sixteen. You end one mana up, no cards drawn, and a board of Vampires.
branches.signals:
Firing your own sweeper tells the table you will burn your engine for damage, which is genuinely intimidating and genuinely expensive information to give away.

It also tells Player 2 that your best rebuild-buster is gone. A control player who was weighing whether to wrath now or later stops weighing.
branches.coalition_risk:
You point everything at the highest life total at the table and leave that player alive around sixteen. That is the specific shape of threat that gets you focused without getting you a kill.

And you do it with no converter, no doubler and no sweeper left, into an untapped control seat. Their wrath still stings them through the drains — but the board it takes is one that can no longer convert a Vampire cast into anything.
branches.coaching:
This is a trap with excellent manners, and the drains improve them — so see where it lies.

The seduction is that the Wrath looks free: your own Corpse Knight and Mondrak dying pay you through Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant. Six drain, six life, feels clever. Count what you bought. Corpse Knight is why Player 3 died this turn and why every future Vampire is three life off every seat. Mondrak is why one token is two. You are selling the conversion layer for six life and thirteen combat damage at a player on thirty-eight.

That kills nobody. Commit exactly as much as wins before the wrath arrives and no further — this commits everything and wins nothing.

Board quality beats board quantity in a four-player game. A pile of 2/2 tokens without the converter behind them is a fair board, and a fair board against two remaining opponents is somebody else's job.

Save Olivia's Wrath for the board it was written for: an opponent's creature deck, with your own non-Vampires either uncast or already spent. It is a one-sided sweeper only on the turn you make it one.

recommendation.choice: Cast Knight of the Ebon Legion, take the kill, and turn the tokens toward Player 2
recommendation.rationale:
One black mana removes a player from the game. There is no version of this turn where that is the wrong first act.

The sweeper fear is the thing worth arguing with, because on this board it points the other way twice. First: your converter and your doubler are creatures, so waiting does not protect them — it only means they die unspent. A converter that has already killed a player is a card you got full value from. Second: Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant turn the wipe itself into your play. Twelve creatures after this turn means a resolved wrath drains each opponent for twelve from Cruel Celebrant, hands Blood Artist twelve more triggers to aim, and gains you twenty-four — point the Artist at the caster and their own sweeper can kill them. The wrath is no longer their exit; it is your second engine.

This is also the assembled game: converter plus multiplier is on the battlefield here, which the record says happens in fifty-seven percent of your games — when the engine shows up, spend it. And nothing in your hand answers a sweeper anyway, so restraint buys you exactly nothing you can name. If the board does go down, Edgar comes off the command zone next turn and rebuilds two bodies at a time.

The direction of the attack is the other half of the call. Player 2 has no creatures and holds the answer; ten damage puts them at twenty and turns their sweeper into a card they need rather than a card they choose. Player 4 has two blockers, thirty-eight life and no interaction showing — let them stay comfortable.

And leave Olivia's Wrath in your hand. Firing it here sells Corpse Knight and Mondrak for six drain and thirteen damage at the wrong seat. That is everything committed for nothing won.

Go now. Take the kill, keep the engine, keep the sweeper — and make the control seat do the arithmetic on a board that charges them by the body.
